section_summary: This section centers on Japan’s postwar population growth, economic resources, public health system, and the promotion of birth control as a means of avoiding hardship and renewed expansionism. It contains a 1945 appeal to General Douglas MacArthur, Warren S. Thompson’s extensive 1949 population-policy report and related correspondence, a newspaper defense of his proposals, and State Department memoranda circulating and evaluating his work. A largely unrelated 1946 Panama Desk routing slip closes the section.

subfiles.title: Letter urging General MacArthur to promote birth control in Japan
subfiles.about: Vickers urges MacArthur to teach and facilitate birth control as a means of reducing Japanese population pressure and preventing future wars.
subfiles.summary: Vickers urges MacArthur to promote birth control, arguing Japan's militarism came from population pressure and food needs, and that family limitation would reduce expansionism.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding “A Population Policy for Japan”
subfiles.about: West sends Butterworth a copy of Warren S. Thompson’s report on population policy in Japan.
subfiles.summary: West forwards Thompson's report 'A Population Policy for Japan' to Butterworth for possible Far Eastern Affairs review.

subfiles.title: Draft letter forwarding Thompson’s supplementary views
subfiles.about: Butterworth prepares to send West a copy of Thompson’s response to State Department questions about Japanese birth control.
subfiles.summary: Draft: Butterworth forwards Thompson's further views, requested by his staff, as worth reading.

subfiles.title: Thompson letter on the prospects for birth control in Japan, first copy
subfiles.about: Thompson evaluates whether Japanese birth control could spread rapidly enough to reduce postwar population growth.
subfiles.summary: Thompson says Japan's low death rate, health centers, midwives and media could speed birth control, but warns overpopulation could bring hardship, disorder and renewed expansionism after US aid ends.

subfiles.title: A Population Policy for Japan
subfiles.to: Chief of the occupation section to which Thompson was attached
subfiles.about: The report assesses Japan’s population-resource imbalance and argues for an explicit policy encouraging a lower birth rate.
subfiles.summary: Thompson surveys Japan’s limited agricultural and mineral resources, damaged industrial base, dependence on imports, and uncertain prospects for earning sufficient foreign exchange through textiles, machinery, and other exports. He argues that higher production and emigration cannot by themselves solve overpopulation and may actually encourage further growth when birth rates remain high. The report concludes that reducing the birth rate is the only durable way to balance population and resources, improve living standards, and diminish incentives for renewed military expansion. It urges American authorities to provide information and advice while leaving voluntary decisions to the Japanese people under their new democratic institutions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 400: Japanese Population Problem
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Tokyo political adviser’s office transmits Thompson’s Nippon Times letter in response to reporting about Soviet criticism of his population proposals.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 400: encloses the May 7 Nippon Times text of Thompson's letter, noting an Izvestiya article about it and Thompson's role as SCAP population adviser.

subfiles.title: “Raps Birth Control Critic: Dr. Thompson Insists His Proposal Is the Only Answer to Overpopulation Here”
subfiles.about: Thompson rebuts Father William S. Kaschmitter’s interpretation of his views and defends birth control as the only permanent solution to Japan’s overpopulation.
subfiles.summary: Thompson says emigration cannot relieve Japan quickly; migration without falling birth rates is futile, and health networks could spread family limitation faster than in the West.

subfiles.title: Thompson letter on the prospects for birth control in Japan, signed copy
subfiles.about: A clean signed copy of Thompson’s assessment of the practical prospects for rapid birth-control adoption in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Signed copy: Thompson cites Japan's low death rate, 700-plus health centers, midwives and government approval for fast spread of family limitation, but warns of hardship and expansion pressure after subsidies end.

subfiles.title: Memorandum requesting Economic Affairs comments
subfiles.to: Mr. Hamilton and the Office of Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Smith asks Economic Affairs whether it has comments on the population paper or subject for transmission to Mr. Rusk.
subfiles.summary: Memo routes the matter via Hamilton and Thorp for Economic Affairs comment, as Rusk had not read the Far Eastern memorandum.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Japanese Population Problem
subfiles.to: W. Walton Butterworth, Mr. Allison, and Mr. Hamilton
subfiles.about: Fearey summarizes Thompson’s report, his own follow-up inquiry, and Thompson’s reply about mass adoption of birth control.
subfiles.summary: Fearey praises Thompson's study of Japan's population problem and asks if ordinary Japanese would use cheap birth control; recommends reading Thompson's reply.

subfiles.title: Letter asking Thompson about mass adoption of birth control
subfiles.about: Fearey asks whether Japanese workers and farmers would practice birth control widely enough to affect population growth.
subfiles.summary: Fearey asks Thompson whether Japanese masses would adopt contraception and for foreign precedents with poor, rapidly growing populations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum transmitting a draft letter to West
subfiles.about: Fearey sends Butterworth the requested draft letter to Robert West enclosing Thompson’s response.
subfiles.summary: Memo transmits a draft letter to West passing Thompson's supplementary discussion to the Department of the Army.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Thompson’s reply to Robert West
subfiles.about: Butterworth sends West a copy of Thompson’s supplementary letter on Japanese population policy.
subfiles.summary: Butterworth sends West Thompson's reply, answering extra points on his earlier study, as worth his attention.

subfiles.title: Thompson letter on the prospects for birth control in Japan, enclosure copy
subfiles.about: This enclosure copy repeats Thompson’s analysis of the likelihood and consequences of rapid birth-control adoption in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Thompson argues Japan's health network and official support could spread contraception to poor families faster than in the West, but doubts Yoshida's commitment and warns of hunger, disorder and expansion after aid ends.

subfiles.title: DC/R routing slip from the Panama Desk
subfiles.to: Internal Department of State distribution offices
subfiles.about: The slip routes a record bearing the reference 894.202/9/7-2246 through several internal offices.
subfiles.summary: DC/R routing slip from the Panama Desk, apparently a stray sheet; action codes, notation dated July 30.
